# Architecture {#sec-architecture}

[Informative]{.status}

This chapter describes the overall shape of the framework: the principles it follows, the participants in it, and how information moves between them.

## Tenets

Safety information should not be confined to proprietary silos
: Information that affects safety at sea must be available to everyone who needs it — individuals, companies and governments alike.
  The framework, its vocabularies and its bindings are openly licensed so that anyone can implement them without permission or fees.

Consistent semantic model
: All participants share one model of what information means (@sec-semantic-model).
  Transports differ; meaning does not.

Transport independence
: No transport is architecturally privileged.
  IP, AIS, NMEA 0183, IEC 61162-450, NMEA 2000 and OneNet are each reached through a binding (Part III), and new transports can be added the same way.

Trust travels with the information
: Authenticity is a property of the information itself, not only of the channel it arrived on (@sec-trust-security).

No central operator
: The framework is a mesh. Anyone can publish, route or consume information; nobody has to operate a central hub.
  The framework itself operates no infrastructure, and in particular none needed at runtime, such as certificate authorities, revocation lists or transparency logs.
  Participants provide these.
  See [provisional decision 0015](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0015-no-framework-infrastructure.md).

Intermittent connectivity is normal
: Links between vessels, and between vessels and shore, are assumed to be intermittent, variable-bandwidth and costly.
  The design must work well when they are.

Existing on-board systems keep working
: The framework adds information to existing navigation workflows.
  It must never make an existing system less safe or less available when the framework is degraded or absent.

## Participants

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Participants and the paths information can take between them (illustrative)."
flowchart LR
  subgraph VA[Vessel A]
    IA[Instruments & displays] --- GA[Gateway]
  end
  subgraph VB[Vessel B]
    GB[Gateway] --- IB[Instruments & displays]
  end
  subgraph Shore
    SA[Shadow of A]
    SB[Shadow of B]
    SVC[Shore services<br/>e.g. authoritative providers,<br/>sighting networks]
  end
  GA -- "IP (when connected)" --- SA
  GB -- "IP (when connected)" --- SB
  SA --- SVC
  SB --- SVC
  SA --- SB
  GA -. "AIS" .- GB
```

Vessel
: A ship or boat taking part in the framework. On board, its instruments and displays communicate over NMEA 0183, NMEA 2000 or other networks.

Gateway
: An on-board component that connects the vessel's own networks to the framework, translating between bindings.

Shadow
: A shore-side representative of a vessel. It holds the vessel's current state, accepts information on its behalf,
  and synchronizes with the vessel whenever a link is available.

Shore service
: Any service ashore that publishes, enriches, routes or consumes information.
  Some are **authoritative** for particular kinds of information; others are contributors.

Client
: Any application that consumes or presents framework information, on board or ashore.

## How information moves

Because links are intermittent and information is plentiful, every participant needs two things:

1. a way to **get the current state** of the things it cares about; and
2. a way to **subscribe to changes** so it can receive timely notifications.

Notification of changes could come from simple polling, or from events raised by the origin of the information or a delegate.
Mechanisms may include HTTP events, MQTT brokers, VHF broadcast or IP multicast.
